listen_text: Chapter. Second-order Logic and Set Theory. Editorial note. This section deals with coding powersets and the continuum in second-order logic. The results are stated but proofs have yet to be filled in. There are no problems yet—and the definitions and results themselves may have problems. Use with caution and report anything that's false or unclear. End editorial note.

Section. Introduction. Since second-order logic can quantify over subsets of the domain as well as functions, it is to be expected that some amount, at least, of set theory can be carried out in second-order logic. By “carry out,” we mean that it is possible to express set theoretic properties and statements in second-order logic, and is possible without any special, non-logical vocabulary for sets (for example, the membership predicate symbol of set theory). For instance, we can define unions and intersections of sets and the subset relationship, but also compare the sizes of sets, and state results such as Cantor's Theorem. End section.

Section. Comparing Sets. Proposition. The formula for every x, if x belongs to capital X, then x belongs to capital Y defines the subset relation, that is, M under assignment s satisfies the formula: for every x, if x belongs to capital X, then x belongs to capital Y if and only if the set assigned to capital X by s is a subset of the set assigned to capital Y by s . End proposition. Proposition. The formula for every x, x belongs to capital X if and only if x belongs to capital Y defines the identity relation on sets, that is, M under assignment s satisfies the formula: for every x, x belongs to capital X if and only if x belongs to capital Y if and only if the set assigned to capital X by s equals the set assigned to capital Y by s . End proposition. Proposition. The formula there exists x belonging to capital X defines the property of being non-empty, that is, M under assignment s satisfies the formula: there exists x belonging to capital X if and only if the set assigned to capital X by s is not empty . End proposition. A set capital X is no larger than a set capital Y , capital X has cardinality at most that of capital Y , if and only if there is an injective function f from capital X to capital Y . Since we can express that a function is injective, and also that its values for arguments in capital X are in capital Y , we can also define the relation of being no larger than on subsets of the domain. Proposition. The formula Displayed expression. there exists a unary function u on the domain such that both of the following hold. First, for every x, if x belongs to capital X, then u of x belongs to capital Y. Second, for all x and y in the domain, if u of x equals u of y, then x equals y. End displayed expression. defines the relation of being no larger than. End proposition. Two sets are the same size, or “equinumerous,” capital X and capital Y are equinumerous , if and only if there is a bijective function f from capital X to capital Y . Proposition. The formula Displayed expression. there exists a unary function u on the domain such that all three conditions hold. First, for every x, if x belongs to capital X, then u of x belongs to capital Y. Second, for all x and y in the domain, if u of x equals u of y, then x equals y. Third, for every y, if y belongs to capital Y, then there exists x belonging to capital X such that y equals u of x. End displayed expression. defines the relation of being equinumerous with. End proposition. Source anomaly note. Source caveat. The displayed function is required to be injective on the entire domain, not just on capital X. Together with its surjectivity from capital X onto capital Y, this is stronger than a bijection between those subsets. For example, a proper countably infinite subset of a countably infinite domain is equinumerous with the domain, but a bijection from that proper subset onto the whole domain cannot extend to an injective function on the whole domain. The displayed formula and claim are preserved, not corrected. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. We will abbreviate these formulas, respectively, as capital X is a subset of capital Y , capital X equals capital Y , capital X is not empty , capital X has cardinality at most that of capital Y , and capital X and capital Y are equinumerous . (This may be slightly confusing, since we use the same notation when we speak informally about sets capital X and capital Y —but here the notation is an abbreviation for formulas in second-order logic involving one-place relation variables capital X and capital Y .) Proposition. The sentence for all subsets capital X and capital Y of the domain, if capital X has cardinality at most that of capital Y and capital Y has cardinality at most that of capital X, then capital X and capital Y are equinumerous is valid. End proposition. Proof. The sentence is satisfied in a structure M if, for any subsets capital X of the domain of M and capital Y of the domain of M , if capital X has cardinality at most that of capital Y and capital Y has cardinality at most that of capital X then capital X and capital Y are equinumerous . But this holds for any sets capital X and capital Y —it is the Schroeder-Bernstein Theorem. End proof. End section.

listen_text: Section. Cardinalities of Sets. Just as we can express that the domain is finite or infinite, enumerable or non-enumerable, we can define the property of a subset of the domain of M being finite or infinite, enumerable or non-enumerable. Proposition. The formula Inf of capital X abbreviates Displayed expression. there exists a unary function u on the domain such that both of the following hold. First, for all x and y in the domain, if u of x equals u of y, then x equals y. Second, there exists y belonging to capital X such that, for every x, if x belongs to capital X, then y is not equal to u of x. End displayed expression. is satisfied with respect to a variable assignment s if and only if the set assigned to capital X by s is infinite. End proposition. Source anomaly note. Source caveat. The formula called Inf does not require u to map capital X into capital X. As printed, a singleton in a two element domain can satisfy it: take u to swap the two elements. Thus the displayed condition does not characterize infinitude as claimed. The source formula is preserved. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Proposition. The formula Count of capital X abbreviates Displayed expression. there exist an element z and a unary function u on the domain such that all three conditions hold. First, z belongs to capital X. Second, for every x, if x belongs to capital X, then u of x belongs to capital X. Third, for every subset capital Y of the domain, if z belongs to capital Y and, for every x, membership of x in capital Y implies membership of u of x in capital Y, then capital X equals capital Y. End displayed expression. is satisfied with respect to a variable assignment s if and only if the set assigned to capital X by s is enumerable. End proposition. Disclosed reader correction. Reader correction. The closing parentheses in the Count display have been balanced around the universally quantified implication and the outer conjunction. No quantifier, connective, or variable has been changed. The exact original remains in Source view. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Source anomaly note. Source caveat. The formula called Count quantifies over every subset capital Y of the domain, then requires equality with capital X whenever capital Y contains z and is closed under u. Taking capital Y to be the whole domain forces capital X to be the whole domain. The formula also requires an element z of capital X and so excludes the empty set. It therefore does not characterize all enumerable subsets as claimed. These mathematical conditions are preserved, not rewritten. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. We know from Cantor's Theorem that there are non-enumerable sets, and in fact, that there are infinitely many different levels of infinite sizes. Set theory develops an entire arithmetic of sizes of sets, and assigns infinite cardinal numbers to sets. The natural numbers serve as the cardinal numbers measuring the sizes of finite sets. The cardinality of denumerable sets is the first infinite cardinality, called aleph zero (“aleph-nought” or “aleph-zero”). The next infinite size is aleph one . It is the smallest size a set can be without being countable (that is, of size aleph zero ). We can define “ capital X has size aleph zero ” as Aleph zero of capital X if and only if both Inf of capital X and Count of capital X . capital X has size aleph one if and only if all its subsets are finite or have size aleph zero , but is not itself of size aleph zero . Hence we can express this by the formula Aleph one of capital X abbreviates the conjunction of two conditions. For every subset capital Y of the domain, if capital Y is a subset of capital X, then either not Inf of capital Y or Aleph zero of capital Y. And not Aleph zero of capital X . Being of size aleph two is defined similarly, etc. Source anomaly note. Source caveat. The proposed Aleph one condition includes capital X among its own subsets. Even if Inf and Aleph zero had their intended meanings, the displayed condition would exclude a set of size aleph one, while allowing finite sets. The definition is preserved as a source defect, not replaced with a new set theoretic characterization. Later claims using this abbreviation inherit the caveat. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. There is one size of special interest, the so-called cardinality of the continuum. It is the size of the power set of the natural numbers , or, equivalently, the size of the real numbers . That a set is the size of the continuum can also be expressed in second-order logic, but requires a bit more work. End section.

listen_text: Section. The Power of the Continuum. In second-order logic we can quantify over subsets of the domain, but not over sets of subsets of the domain. To do this directly, we would need third-order logic. For instance, if we wanted to state Cantor's Theorem that there is no injective function from the power set of a set to the set itself, we might try to formulate it as “for every set capital X , and every set capital P , if capital P is the power set of capital X , then not capital P has cardinality at most that of capital X ”. And to say that capital P is the power set of capital X would require formalizing that the elements of capital P are all and only the subsets of capital X , so something like for every capital Y, capital P applied to capital Y if and only if capital Y is a subset of capital X . The problem lies in capital P applied to capital Y : that is not a formula of second-order logic, since only terms can be arguments to one-place relation variables like capital P . We can, however, simulate quantification over sets of sets, if the domain is large enough. The idea is to make use of the fact that two-place relations capital R relate elements of the domain to elements of the domain. Given such an capital R , we can collect all the elements to which some x is capital R -related: the set of elements y of the domain of M such that capital R relates x to y is the set “coded by” x . Conversely, if capital Z, a subset of the power set of the domain of M, is some collection of subsets of the domain of M , and there are at least as many elements of the domain of M as there are sets in capital Z , then there is also a relation capital R, a subset of the Cartesian square of the domain of M, such that every capital Y in capital Z is coded by some x using capital R . Disclosed reader correction. two-place relations capital R relate elements of the domain to. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Definition. If capital R is a subset of the Cartesian square of the domain of M , then x codes, using capital R, the set of elements y of the domain of M such that capital R relates x to y . End definition. If an element x in the domain of M codes, using capital R, a set capital Z contained in the domain of M , then a set capital Y contained in the domain of M codes a set of sets, namely the sets coded by the elements of capital Y . So a set capital Y can code, using capital R, the power set of capital X . It does so if and only if for every capital Z contained in capital X , some x in capital Y codes, using capital R, capital Z , and every x in capital Y codes, using capital R, a capital Z contained in capital X . Proposition. The formula Displayed expression. Codes applied to x, capital R, and capital Z abbreviates: for every y, y belongs to capital Z if and only if capital R relates x to y. End displayed expression. expresses that the element assigned to x by s codes, using the relation assigned to capital R by s, the set assigned to capital Z by s . The formula Displayed expression. Pow applied to capital Y, capital R, and capital X abbreviates two conditions. First, for every subset capital Z of the domain, if capital Z is a subset of capital X, then there exists x belonging to capital Y such that Codes holds of x, capital R, and capital Z. Second, for every x, if x belongs to capital Y, then for every subset capital Z of the domain, if Codes holds of x, capital R, and capital Z, then capital Z is a subset of capital X. End displayed expression. expresses that the set assigned to capital Y by s codes, using the relation assigned to capital R by s, the power set of the set assigned to capital X by s , that is, the elements of the set assigned to capital Y by s code, using the relation assigned to capital R by s, exactly the subsets of the set assigned to capital X by s . End proposition. Disclosed reader correction. Reader correction. A missing closing parenthesis has been supplied in the final conjunct of the Pow display. The nested implication remains: if x belongs to capital Y, then every subset coded by x using capital R is a subset of capital X. No mathematical condition has been changed. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. With this trick, we can express statements about the power set by quantifying over the codes of subsets rather than the subsets themselves. For instance, Cantor's Theorem can now be expressed by saying that there is no injective function from the domain of any relation that codes the power set of capital X to capital X itself. Proposition. The sentence Displayed expression. for all subsets capital X and capital Y of the domain and all binary relations capital R on the domain: if Pow holds of capital Y, capital R, and capital X, then there does not exist a unary function u on the domain satisfying both conditions. First, for all x and y in the domain, if u of x equals u of y, then x equals y. Second, for every x, if x belongs to capital Y, then u of x belongs to capital X. End displayed expression. is valid. End proposition. The power set of a denumerable set is non-enumerable, and so its cardinality is larger than that of any denumerable set (which is aleph zero ). The size of the power set of the natural numbers is called the “power of the continuum,” since it is the same size as the points on the real number line, the real numbers . If the domain is large enough to code the power set of a denumerable set, we can express that a set is the size of the continuum by saying that it is equinumerous with any set capital Y that codes the power set of set capital X of size aleph zero . (If the domain is not large enough, that is, it contains no subset equinumerous with the real numbers , then there can also be no relation that codes the power set of capital X .) Proposition. If the real numbers have cardinality at most that of the domain of M , then the formula Displayed expression. Cont of capital Y abbreviates: there exist a subset capital X of the domain and a binary relation capital R on the domain such that all three conditions hold. Aleph zero holds of capital X. Pow holds of capital Y, capital R, and capital X. And for all x and y, if x and y both belong to capital Y and, for every z, capital R relates x to z if and only if capital R relates y to z, then x equals y. End displayed expression. expresses that the set assigned to capital Y by s and the real numbers are equinumerous . End proposition. Proof. Pow applied to capital Y, capital R, and capital X expresses that the set assigned to capital Y by s codes, using the relation assigned to capital R by s, the power set of the set assigned to capital X by s , which Aleph zero of capital X says is countable. So the set assigned to capital Y by s is at least as large as the power of the continuum, although it may be larger (if multiple elements of the set assigned to capital Y by s code the same subset of capital X ). This is ruled out by the last conjunct, which requires the association between elements of the set assigned to capital Y by s and subsets of the set assigned to capital Z by s via the relation assigned to capital R by s to be injective. The Continuum Hypothesis is the statement that the size of the continuum is the first non-enumerable cardinality, i.e, that the power set of the natural numbers has size aleph one . Proposition. The Continuum Hypothesis is true if and only if Displayed expression. C H abbreviates: for every subset capital X of the domain, Aleph one of capital X if and only if Cont of capital X. End displayed expression. is valid. End proposition. Note that it isn't true that not C H is valid if and only if the Continuum Hypothesis is false. In an enumerable domain, there are no subsets of size aleph one and also no subsets of the size of the continuum, so C H is always true in an enumerable domain. However, we can give a different sentence that is valid if and only if the Continuum Hypothesis is false: Proposition. The Continuum Hypothesis is false if and only if Displayed expression. End displayed expression. is valid. End proposition. Source anomaly note. Source caveat.
